# Sailing Larger Vessels

*Pages PDF 121-127*

## **Sailing Larger Vessels**
## **Managing the Performance and Morale of Large Crews, and Bigger Boats**
## **Crew Tests**
When dealing with small craft, the basic rules in **Chapter 3: Seafaring** can be used to represent the efforts of a few individuals — such as an adventuring party — keeping a vessel afloat and on course. When dealing with larger vessels, instead of using individual Tests, you can use Crew Tests instead. Crew Tests reflect the many roles and interdependency of activities required to run a ship. Several Characters may contribute to a single Crew Test. The result of a Crew Test is the cumulative total of these individual Tests. 

Once roles are assigned, everyone rolls their individual Test and all the SLs are added together. As with any Test, feel free to assign bonuses and penalties individually or en masse to reflect the conditions. If the total is 1 SL or more, the overall result is a success. The GM may also treat a result of 0 as a success depending on the circumstances. 

Deckhand also serves as a default role for Characters in other roles if those roles are not needed to contribute to a given Crew Test. This is optional — after all, Characters without decent Sail Skills may decide they are better off keeping out of the way of more competent crew. 

## **Vital Roles**
Crew Tests involve crewmembers taking specific roles. The type of Test determines what sort of roles are appropriate. Typical ones are listed below, but they are at the GM’s discretion, and the GM and players should be encouraged to create roles around the available personnel. Everyone should be able to find somewhere to help, even if it’s simply looking out for hazards or holding a rope. 

The GM may decide one of the roles is so vital to the Test that that role counts double. Any SLs, or negative SLs, it generates are therefore doubled. Pertinent vital roles are given in italics for each sample Crew Test.

## **Who Takes a Crew Test?**
The purpose of Crew Tests is to ensure that Characters can still have an influence when a large ship tries to undertake an action, and to spare GMs having to make dozens of rolls in order to work out how the whole crew performs. While any role may be filled by a single person, and certain roles can only be given to individuals, others can be filled by many people at once, especially Lookouts, Deckhands, and Gunners. If one of these is a Character, then that Player could roll to represent everyone performing that role. If there is more than one Character in the same role, they can all roll and use the cumulative total. 

If Characters on board a ship occupy several important roles then there is no need to have NPCs contribute to the Test — the performance of the Characters is representative of the entire crew. However, there are a few circumstances where NPCs may contribute: 

- If a role is not taken by a Character, but can contribute to the Crew Test, and an NPC is available to take on that role. 

- If there is a noteworthy NPC, such as a patron or nemesis, who can take part. 

Instead they should describe to the GM what they are doing to complicate matters, and the GM should impose –1 to –5 SL to the Crew Test depending on the likely negative impact of such machinations. 

Standard profiles for several types of NPC are given on page 127. 

## **Short Handed**
If there are not enough crew to fulfil all the designated roles, then individual crew members may double up on roles. For example, a Deckhand might be running up a sail while also keeping a lookout for rocks, or the Captain might need to take the tiller. Characters in such situations simply make both rolls, but the Difficulty of those rolls is increased by 2 steps to represent their divided attention. 

Even with doubling up, it might not be possible to fulfil the minimum requirements for crew numbers. If this is the case, the results of the Crew Test suffer from –2 SL and may never be more effective than marginally successful. This works for smaller crews where every crew member counts. For larger boats, the modifier only applies for every 10% of the crew that is missing. 

## **Types of Crew Test**

- If the Characters are less competent in a given role than NPCs, or do not wish to undertake the role for some reason. 

If there are NPCs or Characters on board who actively wish to scupper the chances of a Crew Test succeeding for some reason, then they do not take Crew Tests. 

There are several kinds of Crew Tests that can be performed. Many of these will be similar to those that are performed on board smaller ships, but some are unique to vessels with a large, trained crew. 

## **Boat Handling Tests for Progress**
When determining whether a large ship makes good progress in normal conditions, a Crew Test can be made in place of a Boat Handling Test. 

**Roles:** _Captain_ , Chantyman, Deckhand, Helm, Navigator 

## **Boat Handling Tests for Progress in Pursuits**
This sort of Test is all about speed. This is usually done in accordance with the Chasing and Racing rules on page 109. Deckhands trim the sails or man the oars, and so are vital to this task. 

**Roles:** Captain, Chantyman, _Deckhand_ , Helm, Navigator 

## **Boat Handling Tests for Manoeuvres**
Whenever a vessel is called upon to make a Boat Handling Test in order to manoeuvre around a tight bend or obstacle, it can be performed as a Crew Test. The character at the Helm is most important here. 

## **Hard Going**
This sort of Test is required on voyages where the ship has gone too long without sight of land, the objective is uncertain, the seas unknown, if nutrition is a problem, disease has taken hold, or there is some dread about the ship’s prospects. 

**Roles:** Captain, Navigator, Deckhand, _Helm_ , Chantyman 

## **Perception Tests**
Whenever circumstances call for a character on board a vessel to make a Perception Test to spot an oncoming hazard, sight of distant land, or signal from a lighthouse, it can be performed as a Crew Test. A Lookout is most useful here, but speedy reactions from others on deck may help prevent a collision. 

The strains of the journey can begin to show, and crew morale will drop. While Characters can soldier on regardless, NPC crews will start to get uneasy. If the total of this Test results in negative SL, reduce the Morale by that amount in addition to other negative consequences. 

The Hard Going Test is called for under specific circumstances, as noted in the rules for **Extended Voyages** (page 128). 

**Roles:** _Lookout_ , Navigator, Deckhand, Helm, Chantyman 

## **Navigation Tests**
Making sure the ship is on course is the Navigator’s job, though they do benefit from the advice of those on deck. 

**Roles:** Captain, Deckhand, Helm, Lookout, _Navigator_ 

## **Batten Down the Hatches**
Where a smaller vessel would make Boat Handling Tests to avoid damage resulting from strong winds, a larger vessel may benefit from quick decision making by the Captain and swift action by the crew. 

**Roles:** Captain, Lookout, _Deckhand_ , Helm, Chantyman 

## **Pest Control**
Sometimes rats or other pests may infest a ship. In order to deal with the problem, the crew must perform an Extended Pest Control Test. Each Test requires the crew to devote d10 hours to clearing out the vermin. The difficulty and total SL needed to complete the extermination depends on the degree of infestation. A nest of rats on board would require a **Challenging (+0) Extended Pest Control** Test to a total of 10 SL. 

If a Rat Catcher is aboard, they may take the vital role and use their Ranged (Sling) for the Test. The presence of a ship’s cat or small but vicious dog adds +1 SL to the result. 

**Roles:** Captain, Lookout, _Deckhand_ , Helm, Chantyman 

**Roles:** Chantyman, _Cook_ , Navigator, Deckhand, Surgeon 

## **Maintenance**
Smaller vessels can suffer for the want of a trained carpenter, tailor, or boatbuilder when it comes to repairing damage and keeping the ship in good order. A larger vessel can rely on the collective wisdom of its crew to compensate for the lack of any one individual with such skills. 

Any Tests made in order to effect repairs to the ship can be made using the Maintenance Crew Test. 

This Test can be made in place of a Trade Skill needed to repair the boat. However, whilst many hands can help make light of such work, they do not make up for the lack of expert knowledge that a trained carpenter or tailor could provide. As such, if this Crew Test is taken in lieu of such Skills, it suffers from –2 SL. 

**Roles:** Captain, Chantyman, _Deckhand_ , Helm, Navigator 

## **Fire Battery**
If an enemy is within range of the ship’s guns, this Crew Test can be performed if the Captain wishes to unleash a broadside upon them. Rather than rolling to hit for each cannon, the Fire Battery Crew Test can be taken, with the total SL applying to all guns facing the enemy, for better or worse. 

**Roles:** Captain, Chantyman, Deckhand, _Gunner_ , Helm. 

## **Morale**
Extended time at sea is a rotten experience; disease, boredom, and terrible food all combine to erode the mood of any group. The GM should keep track of a ship’s Morale to determine the degree of trust and affection the crew hold towards the captain. 

If the majority of a ship’s crew are highly invested in the voyage, it may not be necessary to track Morale. This may be the case if most of the crew are Player Characters, or if a ship’s crew are zealously devoted to a particular cause or creed. 

However, most large crews are affected by the quality of shipboard life, the performance of their officers, the rewards they can expect from their voyages, and the degree of peril to which they are subjected. A crew that is well led, well victualled, paid regularly, and kept free of danger and disease will likely remain loyal to their captain. A crew that is treated with disrespect, forced to work harder than they might like for scant reward, or that are asked to subsist on starvation rations may well decide to desert the ship, or even take it over. 

Ship Morale typically begins at 75. A new captain with a new crew will typically start at this number. 

Various factors will impact whether this number goes up or down. The following table gives a list of common factors. Morale should be recalculated once every week. When it comes to the behaviour of the captain, the GM should consider their general performance over the previous week. A bad captain may well have skilled lieutenants whose performance makes up for deficiencies. Player Characters may be considered officers for the purposes of Morale if they tend to be vocally (or physically) supportive of the captain. 

The table also reflects the customs and expectations of a crew operating a vessel from the Empire. Those aboard a Norse ship might well expect different things from a captain, particularly when it comes to honouring Manann, or putting up with hardships.

## **Disease**
Disease can sweep through a crew quickly due to the cramped conditions on board and the poor quality of food and drink available to sailors. 

- If a crewmember has a disease with the Coughs and Sneezes symptom, everyone on board is exposed. 

- A crewmember with the Black Plague, Bloody Flux, Galloping Trots, or Itching Pox who drinks from a barrel of water must pass a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test. If the Test is failed, the barrel becomes a source of contagion to anyone who drinks from it later. Small beer is not subject to this rule. 

**Contraction:** Every month without correct nutrition requires a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test. Failure indicates that the Character has contracted scurvy. If the Character regularly eats fermented cabbage broth they make an **Easy (+40) Endurance** Test to resist contraction. 

**Duration:** The disease persists until 1d10 days after regularly eating fresh fruit and vegetables. 

**Symptoms:** Flux, Malaise, Nausea, Wounded. 1% chance of losing a tooth each day. 

## **Sea Sickness**
Most folk get seasick when they first sail, but anyone who sticks around will grow out of it. Elves tend to be immune, to the irritation of Dwarf sailors. 

**Contraction:** Whenever any Human, Dwarf, Halfling, or Ogre Character first undertakes a journey at sea, they must make a **Difficult (–10) Endurance** Test or suffer from sea sickness. In rough weather (Strong Gales or Violent Storms), such Characters should make a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test or suffer from sea sickness. 

**Duration:** For sea sickness due to being new to seafaring, make a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test after each day at sea. If the Test is passed, the Character will not suffer this form of sea sickness again. For sea sickness resulting from rough seas or other temporary effects, make a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test every hour. 

**Symptoms:** Malaise, Nausea. 

## **Provisions**
## **Scurvy**
Scurvy can afflict those who stay away from shore for extended periods. The cause of the disease is unclear. Bretonnian thought is that spending too long away from their beloved Bretonnia is naturally bad for you. Some blame it on weakness of character. 

The disease starts with weariness, weakness, and ennui. Then it progresses to spontaneous bleeding and thinning blood which can turn into open sores. Then the sufferer’s bones weaken, and their teeth fall out. 

The careful planning of any long voyage is vital to its success, especially when it comes to supplies. The hard work required of any crew means that a lot of food and water is required to keep them fit. A captain should know that just buying any available food in the marketplace risks disaster on a long expedition as it soon goes putrid. 

## **Barrel of Fresh Water**
Fresh water is usually stored in great barrels and doled out carefully. A good captain knows to make sure the ship is over-supplied, especially on voyages into unknown seas. On such a voyage, a captain should take every opportunity to replenish their supply. A barrel contains 32 gallons of water. A member of a crew drinks a gallon per day.

## **Barrel of Small Beer**
Sometimes small beer is used instead of water; this helps keep the water uncontaminated, and though the beer is alcoholic, it is so dilute as to be hydrating. A barrel of water and a keg of ale can produce a barrel of small beer. The Bretonnian Navy uses diluted wine instead. 

## **Day’s Ration of Hard Tack**
The famous ship’s biscuit, or hardtack, is important as it provides much needed calories, is cheap to make, compact and light for storage, and lasts a long time without spoiling. It is hard as rock, however, and requires soaking before it can be easily eaten. The weevils that infest the biscuits are just extra nutrition. Hard tack is all that is needed to stave off starvation, though it is a poor diet. 

## **Compass**
A rudimentary compass made from a needle balanced on a pin. Navigation Tests benefit from +1 SL with the aid of a compass. 

## **Sealskin**
A sealskin overcoat keeps its wearer warm and dry. They usually come with over-mittens which are great for keeping hands warm but make dextrous acts impossible. A good sealskin can give a bonus of +1 SL to Endurance Tests made to resist cold exposure. 

## **Ship Parts**
‘Ship parts’ is a collective term covering timbers shaped to fit the hull, pitch to waterproof the boat, rope to repair the rigging and cloth to patch the sails. Ship parts are used up when undertaking the _Ship Maintenance_ Endeavour. 

## **Hirelings**
Getting a crew together is a costly business. The Hirelings rules from **Up in Arms** can be used to add quick detail and quirks to individual Hirelings, but the following NPCs are commonly seen amongst a ship’s crew. 

## Prize Money
As well as regular pay, the crew of a ship expect prize money — a share of the loot taken from any captured enemy vessels. Prize money is traditionally split the following way: 50% to the owner of the vessel (or spent on keeping the vessel provisioned and maintained), 10% to the captain, and 40% split among the remaining crew. Officers tend to forgo prize money, as do noncombatants such as Doktors or Huffers. 

## **Day’s Ration of Preserves**
Preserving and storing the large quantities of food required on a voyage is a problem. Salting meat is one effective preservative. Pickling vegetables is common, using vinegar, alcohol, or sugar. 

## **Day’s Ration of Fermented Cabbage Broth**
Fermented cabbage broth tastes awful and crews dislike it immensely. The Imperial Navy has recently decreed that those who do not imbibe their daily ration are to be flogged. This still does not stop seamen throwing theirs overboard when officers are not looking. Any ship’s cook able to make this broth appetising is much sought after.
